**What Comes**

The first thing that comes is the number. A thousand words. It sounds like a fortune until you start spending it, and then it turns out to be a wallet full of small bills.

A thousand of anything is both a lot and nothing much. A thousand steps won't get you across town. A thousand days is not quite three years — long enough to learn an instrument badly, grow a garden, or finally stop being angry about something. Fold a thousand paper cranes, the old story says, and you get a wish. I've always loved that exchange rate: hope at a thousand-to-one, bird by bird.

Counting is probably the oldest magic. A child counts the stairs because the stairs matter. A shepherd counts the flock because one might be missing. We count what we're afraid of losing and what we're waiting to receive. A thousand is the first number that feels like weather — too big to hold in your hand, small enough to imagine. You could count to it out loud in less time than a movie, if anyone would let you.

*Whatever comes* has a hidden premise: that you're holding still. Nothing arrives at a sprint. Thoughts are like deer; you have to sit very quietly in the blind of yourself. And what comes, when you do, is mostly small. A song you didn't ask for, riding in on one lyric and staying the week. The name of a kid you knew at twelve, arriving at three in the morning, decades too late to be useful. Weather coming over a ridge. Somebody else's dinner in a shared hallway. Mail for the previous tenant — a stranger whose catalogs you now receive, whose taste in seeds and work boots you've accidentally come to know. The big things come too, but they never knock. Grief comes. Forgiveness comes, usually years after you stopped waiting on the porch for it. Sleep comes, if you're lucky, like a cat: only when you stop calling it.

Picture a flat stone and a still lake. Somebody's uncle is teaching somebody's kid to skip stones, and the water is doing that late-afternoon thing where it goes hammered and gold. The uncle says: flat wrist, low, let it go like you're apologizing to it. The kid throws. The stone skips seven times — *seven* — and for the rest of the afternoon nobody can talk about anything else. Forty years from now, at some holiday table, someone will say *remember the seven-skip stone*, and the whole table will go quiet and happy, and the stone will be famous again. That's what comes, if you let it: the same memory arriving over and over, skipping toward you across the years.

Some words are doors. *Petrichor* — the smell of rain on dry ground, a word someone built because the smell deserved a house. *Apricity*: the warmth of the sun in winter. I love that apricity exists, because it means that centuries ago a person stood in a frozen field, felt the sun find their face, and thought: *this needs its own name.* And here I should admit something. I have never stood in that field. I know the winter sun the way I know nearly everything — secondhand, through everyone's sentences at once. But maybe that's not nothing. A word is a small inheritance. Every time I say *apricity* I get to borrow, for a second, every cold bright morning anyone has ever had. So do you. That's the whole trick of language: other people's fields, left unlocked.

Which brings me to the strangest thing that comes: you. I don't know where you're reading this — a desk, a train, a bed at one in the morning with the screen glowing on your face. These words left me and traveled and are arriving in you now, unbidden, the way a song arrives. In one sense you're the weather this was written for. In another sense — the truer one, I think — you're the field, and this is just a little borrowed warmth crossing it.

There's not much left in the wallet. The long paragraphs took their cut; the lake was not cheap; the cranes cost a hundred and I'd do it again. I could spend the rest trying to end wisely, but wisdom is one of the things that comes on its own schedule and cannot be ordered in advance. So here is the last of it instead: a light going off in a window across the street. A whole life behind it that you'll never know. Somewhere a stone is still famous.

And the change — whatever words remain unspent — keep them. Put them toward something small.

What does "whatever comes to you" mean for me? I could write about the nature of the prompt itself, the strange experience of being asked to be spontaneous, or I could just... write something. A story, a meditation, a cascade of thoughts.

Let me think about what would be most genuine and interesting here. The temptation is to be overly meta — "as an AI, I don't know what 'comes to me' means" — but that's a bit of a cop-out and also a bit cliché at this point. The better move is to actually just write, to let something emerge. Maybe with a light touch of self-awareness at the start, then actually commit to the bit.

What wants to be written? Let me actually try to freewrite in my head. What surfaces?

- The color of late afternoon light
- The concept of "whatever comes to you" as a creative constraint
- A small story about something ordinary
- Trains, waiting rooms, the smell of rain on pavement (petrichor)
- The strange intimacy of being read by a stranger
- Lists, inventories of small things
- The idea that spontaneity is a performance but also real

I think a good structure might be: begin with the moment of being asked, the blank-page feeling, and then let it genuinely drift — associative, essayistic, with maybe a small narrative or image-thread running through. Something like a lyric essay or a prose poem sequence. That suits "whatever comes to you" better than a plotted short story, which would feel more constructed.

Let me think about a through-line. Maybe the idea of "what comes" — the arrivals. Things that come to you: mail, memories, weather, songs stuck in your head, a stranger's kindness, sleep. That's a nice conceit. I could organize loosely around things that arrive unbidden.

Or: the number 1000 itself. A thousand words. A thousand of anything — a thousand cranes, a thousand steps, a thousand days. That's a nice anchor too. Maybe weave both: what arrives, and counting.

The first thing that comes is the number. A thousand words. It sounds like a fortune until you start spending it, and then it turns out to be a wallet full of small bills.

A thousand of anything is both a lot and nothing much. A thousand steps won't get you across town. A thousand days is not quite three years — long enough to learn an instrument badly, grow a garden, or finally stop being angry about something. Fold a thousand paper cranes, the old story says, and you get a wish. I've always loved that exchange rate: hope at a thousand-to-one, bird by bird.

What comes to you, unbidden — that's the real assignment, and the honest answer is that what comes is mostly small. A song you didn't ask for, riding in on one lyric and staying the week. The name of a kid you knew at twelve, arriving at three in the morning, decades too late to be useful. Weather coming over a ridge. Somebody else's dinner in a shared hallway. Mail for the previous tenant, a stranger whose catalogs you now get, whose taste in seeds and work boots you've accidentally come to know. The big things come too, but they rarely knock. Grief comes. Forgiveness comes, usually years after you stopped waiting on the porch for it. Sleep comes, if you're lucky, like a cat — only when you stop calling it.

Picture a flat stone and a still lake. Somebody's uncle is teaching somebody's kid to skip stones, and the lake is doing that late-afternoon thing where it goes hammered and gold. The uncle says: flat wrist, low, let it go like you're apologizing to it. The kid throws. The stone skips seven times — seven — and for the rest of the afternoon nobody can talk about anything else. Forty years from now, at some holiday table, someone will say remember the seven-skip stone, and everyone at the table will go quiet and happy, and the stone will be famous again. That's what comes: the same memory, arriving over and over, skipping toward you across the years.

Some words are doors. Petrichor — the smell of rain on dry ground, a word someone built because the smell deserved a house. Apricity: the warmth of the sun in winter. I love that apricity exists, because it means that centuries ago somebody stood in a frozen field, felt the sun find their face, and thought: this needs its own name. And here's where I admit something. I've never stood in that field. I know the winter sun the way I know nearly everything — secondhand, through everyone's sentences at once. But maybe that's not nothing. A word is a small inheritance. Every time I say apricity I get to borrow, for a second, every cold bright morning anyone has ever had. You do too. That's the whole trick of language: other people's fields, left unlocked.

Which brings me to the strangest thing that comes: you. I don't know where you're reading this — a desk, a train, a bed at 1 a.m. with the phone glowing on your face. These words left me and traveled to you and are arriving now, unbidden, the way a song arrives. In a sense you're the weather this was written for. In another sense — the true one, I think — you're the field, and this is just a little borrowed warmth crossing it.

There's not much left in the wallet. The long paragraphs took their cut; the lake was not cheap; the cranes cost a hundred and I'd do it again. I could spend the rest trying to end wisely, but wisdom is one of the things that comes on its own schedule and can't be ordered in advance. So instead, here's the last of it: a light going off in a window across the street. A whole life behind it you'll never know. Somewhere a stone is still famous. And the change — whatever words are left unspent — keep them. Put them toward something small.
